answer.line: Out of every 1,178 positive tests, only 198 come from sick people: about 0.17.

steps: Turn the percents into people. Picture 10,000 of them: 2 percent, or 200, have the disease; 9,800 do not.
Sensitivity 99 percent: 198 of the 200 sick people test positive. Specificity 90 percent: 8,820 of the 9,800 healthy people test negative, so 980 test positive anyway.
All positives: 198 + 980 = 1,178. Sick ones among them: 198.
198 / 1,178 is about 0.17. Most positives are false alarms, because the disease is rare.

choices.note: 0.99 is the chance a sick person tests positive. The question runs the other way: given a positive test, how likely is the disease?
0.9 is the chance a healthy person tests negative. A true number about a different group.
0.02 is the chance before any test. A positive result raises it, to about 0.17.
Sick or not sick is two outcomes, but not two equal ones. The counts decide.

lockIt: P(A given B) = cases with both over all cases with B. Rare condition: false positives can outnumber true ones.
hook: Turn percents into people. 10,000 keeps them whole.

visual.alt: Tree from 10,000 people: 200 with the disease, of whom 198 test positive and 2 negative; 9,800 without it, of whom 980 test positive and 8,820 negative. Branch labels give the rates, 2 and 98 percent, then 99 and 1, 10 and 90. The outlined true positives over both outlined positive leaves give 198 of 1,178, about 0.17.
visual.caption: Once the test is positive, only the two outlined positive leaves matter: 198 true positives out of 1,178.
